summary: The note analyzes how consumers and institutions behaved during a prolonged internet outage that began September 20, 2023 and lasted nearly two weeks. It covers effects on remote work, commerce, social life, mental health, entertainment, education, small businesses and emergency services. It concludes that the outage exposed society's digital dependence and raised questions about provider preparedness and internet access as a basic right.
one_line: Report on how consumers, businesses, schools and services coped with a nearly two-week internet outage starting September 20, 2023.
key_facts: The outage began in the early hours of September 20, 2023, affecting residents across several counties and leaving thousands without internet access.
Reports suggested the causes were a combination of infrastructural failure and cyber-attacks.
Freelance graphic designer Sarah Jennings, like other telecommuters, faced missed deadlines and financial losses within the first 48 hours.
Steven Matthis, owner of a local bakery, saw sales dip because the outage disabled his card-payment facilities.
MaryAnne Briscoe, a high school teacher, observed her students engaging more during break times, initially out of boredom.
Dr. Richard Lively, a mental health professional, noted increased anxiety and stress from digital withdrawal, alongside some reports of relief and 'forced' relaxation.
Zoe Carter, mother of two, kept her family entertained with old DVDs and board games.
University professor Russell Grant remarked on disparities in students' ability to cope, reflecting unequal access to technology.
Local grocers tracked sales and inventory manually and used community social media groups over mobile data to update customers.
Community leader Elena Morris advocated categorizing internet access alongside water and electricity as essential.
Emergency services, including first responders and hospitals, were strained because they rely heavily on digital systems for communication and information management.
Connectivity was largely restored after nearly two weeks of sustained effort, in early October 2023.
Telecommunications companies faced criticism from customers and regulators over lack of comprehensive backup plans.
